Observations of Duckbill catfish (Sorubim lima) from the lower Amazon floodplain provide a detailed view of its early life history. Egg diameter estimates, derived from the closely related congener Hemisorubim platyrhynchos, suggest that at first emergence from the chorion, the prolarvae weigh approximately 0.0028 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0028 grams]. This minute wet weight at birth, comparable to a small grain of sand, underscores the highly altricial state of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the duration of the endotrophic yolk-sac stage is surprisingly brief; hatching occurs just 11 days [ab = 11 days] after fertilization. This compressed incubation period is typical of many tropical Siluriformes that spawn during the rising-water season, where rapid development offers a selective advantage against predation on the vulnerable egg and prolarval stages. The transition from lecithotrophy to the onset of exogenous feeding is therefore a critical and energetically demanding window in the species' ontogeny.

As the pelagic larvae grow and eventually undergo larval metamorphosis, their somatic trajectory becomes closely tied to seasonal trophic pulses. A comprehensive survey of adults captured in gillnet sets across the mainstem, floodplain lakes, and connecting channels indicates that the ultimate total length attained by Sorubim lima is 54.2 centimeters [Li = 54.2 centimeters]. This maximum asymptotic size places the species among the medium-bodied pimelodids, considerably smaller than the massive Brachyplatystoma genus but notably larger than many other members of the family. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight predicted from a length-weight relationship established for the population reaches 1.25 kilograms [Wwi = 1.25 kilograms]. This substantial adult body mass, combined with its elongated, duckbill-like snout, reflects an adaptation for suction-feeding on small fish and decapods in turbid, low-visibility habitats. The body plan of these sexually mature adults is streamlined for sustained swimming in the main river channel.

The transition to reproductive activity is governed by a relatively early size threshold. Examination of gonadal development in a sample of 187 individuals collected over two hydrological cycles revealed the total length at puberty to be 23.2 centimeters [Lp = 23.2 centimeters], a size corresponding to approximately the second year of growth under typical floodplain conditions. At this length, the estimated wet weight at puberty derived from the species-specific length-mass equation is 87.95 grams [Wwp = 87.95 grams]. This modest body mass at the onset of gametogenesis suggests an opportunistic life-history strategy in which females can allocate energy to vitellogenesis relatively soon after completing the most rapid phase of juvenile growth. The population-level gonadosomatic index (GSI) for females, calculated from gravid individuals at the height of the spawning season, averages 15% [GSI = 15%] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

Long-term mark-recapture data collected over a decade in the Amazon River system provide robust evidence for the species’ overall longevity. The maximum recorded lifespan observed in a single large male recaptured in a floodplain lake near Santarém was 6 years [am = 6 years] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], corresponding to approximately 2,190 days. This longevity is moderate for a South American pimelodid, falling well short of the multi-decade spans reported for some large Amazonian catfishes but exceeding the rapid turnover typical of small characins. The survivorship curve inferred from the recapture data shows a relatively constant annual mortality rate between the juvenile and adult stages, with senescence-related mortality becoming apparent only after the fifth year. The 6-year maximum lifespan (6 years) [am = 6 years] thus anchors the species' pace of life as a moderately iteroparous strategist, balancing the energetic demands of multiple annual spawning events against the risk of predation and habitat variability at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

From a comparative perspective, the reproductive biology of Sorubim lima aligns well with that of other medium-sized tropical pimelodids, though its relatively early maturation is a distinguishing trait. Where many congeners delay first spawning until reaching lengths well above 30 centimeters, this species initiates gametogenesis at a total length of just 23.2 centimeters [Lp = 23.2 centimeters], a strategy that allows earlier reproductive contribution in the dynamic floodplain environment. The corresponding wet weight at first sexual development of 87.95 grams [Wwp = 87.95 grams] serves as a useful benchmark for bioenergetic models of the regional ichthyofauna, and when combined with the species' moderately iteroparous spawning schedule—typically timed to rising water levels that enhance larval survival—it underscores an opportunistic life-history adapted to unpredictable hydrological conditions. The maximum adult body size, defined by a total length of 54.2 centimeters [Li = 54.2 centimeters] and an asymptotic mass of 1.25 kilograms [Wwi = 1.25 kilograms], places Sorubim lima within a distinct niche among Amazonian pimelodids, bridging the gap between small-bodied forage fish and the long-lived migratory giants of the basin.
